title: Gus the T. rex Hits the Auction Block: Will a Museum or Billionaire Snag the $30 Million Skeleton?
summary: Picture a creature as long as a city bus and as tall as a one-story building, with teeth the size of bananas. That’s Gus, a Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton going up for auction at Sotheby’s in New York City on Tuesday. The starting bid? A cool $19 million, with an estimated final price of $20–30 million. Gus was unearthed in 2021 on private land in Harding County, South Dakota, by Theropoda Expeditions. The skeleton is 38 feet long and 12.5 feet tall, dating back 67 million years to the late Cretaceous period. It’s named after Gary “Gus” Licking, the rancher who owned the land. He had found T. rex teeth and fossil fragments for years before the excavation began. Tragically, he died during the dig, which lasted until 2023, and never saw the fully assembled skeleton. According to Sotheby’s, nearly a thousand pieces were collected, making Gus one of the largest and most complete T. rex specimens ever discovered. This isn’t the first dinosaur auction. In 1997, Sotheby’s sold Sue the T. rex for $8.4 million to the Field Museum in Chicago. More recently, in 2024, Apex the stegosaurus fetched a staggering $44.6 million from billionaire Ken Griffin, who loaned it to the American Museum of Natural History. The trend worries some paleontologists. Scott Persons, curator of natural history at the South Carolina State Museum, notes that such sums could instead fund decades of research and public exhibitions. “A sum like that could endow a research program at a public museum of your choosing,” he says. “That would pay for a career’s worth of fieldwork, the discovery of whole new species, and the public exhibition of the findings.” As the gavel falls, the question remains: will Gus end up in a public institution or a private collection?
why_it_matters: The fate of fossils like Gus raises fundamental questions about who owns Earth's prehistoric past and whether rare scientific treasures should be available to all in museums or locked away in private galleries, potentially shaping the careers of future paleontologists and the public's understanding of natural history.

background_read: Tyrannosaurus rex roamed western North America during the late Cretaceous period, which ended about 66 million years ago with the mass extinction that wiped out all non-avian dinosaurs. It was one of the largest land predators ever, with a bite force strong enough to crush bones. The first partial T. rex skeleton was discovered in 1902, and fewer than 40 relatively complete specimens have been unearthed since.

The commercialization of dinosaur fossils has accelerated in recent decades. Sue the T. rex, found in 1990 on Native American trust land, sparked a legal battle over ownership before being auctioned in 1997 to the Field Museum in Chicago (one of the largest natural history museums in the world) for $8.4 million—then the highest price ever paid for a fossil.

Ken Griffin (the founder of the hedge fund Citadel and one of the richest people in the United States) purchased Apex in 2024 for $44.6 million, demonstrating a new era of ultra-wealthy individuals entering the fossil market. He loaned it to the American Museum of Natural History in New York City for public display.

Theropoda Expeditions, the company that excavated Gus, is a commercial fossil hunting firm. Such companies often sell specimens at auctions, which can draw criticism from academic paleontologists who fear that scientifically valuable fossils may disappear into private collections where researchers and the public cannot access them.

perspectives.description: Auction supporters, including commercial fossil hunters, say high prices encourage more people to search for and properly excavate fossils that might otherwise erode away unnoticed. A sale to a museum, even at a high price, guarantees the specimen will be preserved and displayed for public education. Private owners sometimes also loan fossils to museums, as Ken Griffin did.

Many researchers argue that critical fossils belong in public trust institutions, not in the hands of wealthy collectors who can deny scientists access for study. When prices climb into the tens of millions, it becomes almost impossible for museums—often funded by limited grants—to compete, meaning scientifically important specimens may vanish from the academic record.

The legal framework in the United States allows landowners to sell fossils found on their property, unlike many other countries where fossils are state property. This has created a booming market and a long-running debate over whether dinosaur bones should be considered natural heritage rather than private commodities. The commercial fossil trade is now a multi-million dollar industry that shows no signs of slowing.

If major museums and universities cannot afford to bid, they may have to form international consortiums or rely on wealthy donors to secure fossils. New laws or ethical guidelines could emerge to limit the sale of scientifically unique specimens, but any such change would face strong opposition from landowners and commercial diggers. The next decade may see more fossils ending up in private hands, changing the landscape of paleontology permanently.
